                        High-accuracy physical property prediction for pure organics via molecular representation learning: bridging data to discovery

                    AbstractThe escalating energy crisis has spurred extensive research into organic compounds for energy-efficient applications, taking advantage of their environmental friendliness, cost-effective synthesis, and adaptable molecular structures. Traditional trial-and-error methods for discovering highly functional organic compounds are expensive and time-consuming. We employed a 3D transformer-based molecular representation learning algorithm to create the Org-Mol pre-trained model, using 60 million semi-empirically optimized small organic molecule structures. After fine-tuning with public experimental data, the model can accurately predict various physical properties of pure organics, with test set R2 values exceeding 0.92. These fine-tuned models are used in high-throughput screening among millions of ester molecules to identify novel immersion coolants, resulting in the experimental validation of two promising candidates. This work not only demonstrates the potential of Org-Mol in predicting bulk properties for pure organic compounds but also paves the way for the rational and efficient development of ideal candidates for energy-saving materials.

                            IntroductionAmidst the current energy crisis, the research and development of materials that are energy-efficient and/or offer high energy utilization efficiency have become an immediate imperative and a focal point in scientific inquiry1,2,3,4. Organic compounds play a pivotal role in this context, owing to their environmental friendliness, low-cost processing, and almost infinite modifiability to meet a wide array of property requirements. Prospective applications lie in the fields such as immersion coolants for data centers5,6,7, phase change materials for thermal energy storage8,9, and liquid organic hydrogen carriers10,11,12. All of these fields raise specific requirements on various physical and chemical properties of the applied organics. Taking immersion coolants for the data center as an example, an ideal coolant should possess a low dielectric constant and viscosity, as well as high heat capacity and thermal conductivity, so as to provide a high thermal exchange efficiency during the circulation while preventing plausible signal loss during the operation of electronic devices13,14.Although the measurement of the properties mentioned above for a single compound is straightforward15, the synthesis of various candidates can be time-consuming. Therefore, the experimental trial-and-error cost of exploring the chemical space to develop ideal energy-saving organic materials remains high. Multiple attempts have been made to predict these electrical, mechanical, and thermal properties of organic compounds via molecular dynamics (MD) and/or machine learning (ML) methods16,17,18,19,20,21,22,23,24. However, the accuracy of such methods relies on the applied force field and/or the algorithm applied in the ML model, as well as the quality and the size of the data set25,26,27. It can be seen that predicting these physical properties via MD is time-consuming for a single system16 and becomes unaffordable in a high-throughput screening scenario with thousands of candidates, while the validity of some previously reported ML models is limited to a few specific types of compounds20,23,28. The requirement of constructing the appropriate descriptors for ML models can also be computationally expensive and sometimes non-trivial19,21,27,29, raising additional challenges for making an accurate yet efficient predictio,n which is generalizable to a plethora of organic compounds.With the development of deep learning algorithms, highly efficient screening and rational design of novel materials with required properties have been further made simple30,31,32. For instance, Uni-Mol, a 3D transformer-based molecular representation learning (MRL) algorithm33, has been successfully applied in the prediction of photophysical properties of organic photoluminescence systems34 and the adsorption energies of various gaseous molecules on metal-organic-frameworks35. One of the most favored advantages of Uni-Mol is that sufficient and rational descriptors can be automatically constructed via the pre-training process, requiring only a single molecular structures as input, and the pre-trained model can be further optimized by the subsequent fine-tuning with a small number of labeled data33,34,35. While most of the previously reported properties predicted by the Uni-Mol framework depend solely on a single molecular structure or on a single cell of a periodic crystallized structure, its feasibility in predicting bulk properties for amorphous (or liquid phase) organic compounds is yet to be validated. If proven effective, such a protocol may remarkably streamline the model-constructing process and reduce the computational cost in predicting a variety of physical properties for pure amorphous organics.Keeping these in mind and to facilitate the discovery of energy-saving materials in terms of pure organics, we apply the Uni-Mol framework to develop a pre-trained model specifically designed for organic compounds, namely, the Org-Mol model, followed by the fine-tuning process over various physical properties with public experimental data. Our results show that even though only the single molecular coordinates are provided during the pre-training process, the fine-tuned models for all bulk properties of pure organic small molecules achieve significantly high accuracy (with the R2 value of the test set higher than 0.95). As a proof-of-concept, we also assess how effectively Org-Mol can fine-tune the glass transition temperature of homopolymers using the structure of the repeating unit as input, achieving an R2 score above 0.92 on the test set. Notably, these fine-tuned models are applied in a high-throughput screening for the discovery of novel immersion coolants over millions of ester molecules. Hundreds of candidates are finally filtered out, and two of them are experimentally synthesized and validated, highlighting the capability of Org-Mol to directly bridge data to discovery. Notwithstanding that the current study focuses on single-component organic systems, the prediction framework established here can be readily adapted to other energy-saving materials (e.g., phase-change materials) via the same fine-tuning process.ResultsPre-trained model and fine-tuning data setsWe first perform a t-SNE analysis36 for the molecular weight of the pre-training data set to speculate the effectiveness of Org-Mol pre-trained model in learning molecular structures and its ability to distinguish between different molecules. The 512-dimension embedding layer of the Org-Mol model is projected into two dimensions, and the distributions of the molecular weight of 20,000 randomly selected molecules in the pre-training data are shown in Fig. 1a and b. With the randomly initialized weight (as shown in Fig. 1a), the data points are more evenly distributed, while in Fig. 1b, where the Org-Mol pre-trained weight is applied, the data points with similar molecular weights tend to cluster together, elucidating that a simple structure-property relationship has been constructed by the Org-Mol pre-trained model. As detailed in Fig. 1c, to accurately predict physical properties of various organic compounds, we carry out the fine-tuning process for each physical property of interest so that a more specific and sophisticated structure-property relationship can be established. The size and range of each property are summarized in Table 1.Fig. 1: Org-Mol model’s pretraining dataset’s molecular weight distribution via t-SNE analysis and the pre-training/fine-tuning process.Full size imagea, b Distributions of the molecular weight of the pre-training dataset in 2D projections of Org-Mol embedding layer via t-SNE with a randomly initialized weight and the Org-Mol pretrained weight, respectively. c Schematic graph of the pre-training and fine-tuning process of the Org-Mol model for organic compounds.Table 1 Dataset size and value ranges of the fine-tuning dataset used in this study, including dielectric constant ε near 25 °C, kinematic viscosity ν at 40 °C and 100 °C, density ρ at 40 °C, the specific heat at constant pressure Cp at 25 °C, and thermal conductivity κ at 25 °C for organic small molecules, and the glass transition temperature Tg of homopolymersFull size tablePrediction of the electrical propertyThe dielectric constant is chosen as a representative to validate the performance of Org-Mol on predicting the electrical property, which plays a crucial role in the field of energy materials, especially in the areas of electrochemical energy storage as well as the development of novel immersion coolants37. The static dielectric constant ε of a given system is the value of the frequency-dependent dielectric function in the limit of zero frequency38. The numerical value of εS can be evaluated via the fluctuations of the total dipole moment of the system, which equals the summation of the molecular dipole moments (μi), i.e., M = ∑iμi. Mathematically, one has39,40$$\varepsilon =1+\frac{\left\langle {{\bf{M}}}^{2}\right\rangle -{\left\langle {\bf{M}}\right\rangle }^{2}}{3{\epsilon }_{0}V{k}_{{\rm{B}}}T}$$
                    (1)
                where ϵ0 is vacuum permittivity, V the volume, kB the Boltzmann constant, and T the temperature. For systems with a totally random and uncorrelated arrangement of dipoles, \({\left\langle {\bf{M}}\right\rangle }^{2}=0\) and ε are proportional to the square of the average molecular dipole moment. However, such straight forward relationship between the static dielectric constant of a bulk organic system and the molecular dipole moment can merely be satisfied in practice due to the unpredictable orientation of the single molecular dipoles. As shown in Fig. 2a, the correlation coefficient (R) between the square of the computed single molecular dipole moment (without averaging over different configurations) and the experimental dielectric constant is only 0.728. A few conspicuous outliers are those with a hydroxyl group and/or an amino group (as labeled in Fig. 2a), which introduce the formation of the hydrogen bond and the corresponding oriented arrangement of the dipoles. Consequently, the single molecular dipole moment, despite being straightforward to calculate, is not an appropriate metric, especially for a quantitative evaluation of the static dielectric constant. It should be noted that previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of accurately computing the dielectric constant for organic systems using MD simulations via a delicate approach to extract the short-ranged Kirkwood g-factor16,41. Though with high accuracy, such calculations usually require remarkably long simulation time for a single system (especially for those large flexible organics), and are merely affordable to be applied in high high-throughput screening process.Fig. 2: Org-Mol model’s performance in predicting dielectric constant and related analyses.Full size imagea The experimental dielectric constant with respect the the square of the calculated molecular dipole moment of randomly picked systems. Dashed green line denotes the linear fit and shaded area denotes three standard deviations. b, c The correlation between Org-Mol predicted dielectric constants and experimental counterparts for the training set and the test set, respectively. d Electrostatic charge distribution and molecular dipole moment of butanoic acid, methyl propanoate, ethyl acetate, and propyl methanoate (from top to bottom). e Snapshots of the MD simulation of butanoic acid that indicates the existence of the dimer structure.Although the static dielectric constant is a bulk property, its value for various organic compounds can be accurately predicted via the Org-Mol fine-tuned model with only the single molecular coordinates as the input. As shown in Fig. 2b, for the static dielectric constant near room temperature, the R2 value of the training set is 0.990, and that of the test set is around 0.968, with an MAE of 0.726 (as shown in Fig. 2c). While most of the compounds in the data set are liquids, we further validate Org-Mol’s applicability in organic semiconductors. As shown in Table S1, we compare the dielectric constants of three organic semiconductors (structures given in Fig. S3) predicted by Org-Mol with their experimental values. For all three organic semiconductors, Org-Mol provides reasonable predictions as compared to the experimental values. The capability of Org-Mol to predict bulk properties from single-molecule inputs arises from its unique integration of Uni-Mol’s 3D transformer architecture and fine-tuning with experimental measured properties. During pre-training, the model implicitly learns geometric patterns (e.g., bond angles, atomic distances) from 60 million PM6-optimized single-molecule structures, capturing latent structural motifs associated with intermolecular interactions like hydrogen bonding or dipole-dipole forces. However, challenges persist because single-molecule representations lack explicit information about condensed-phase dynamics, such as dipole correlations governing the dielectric constant (as shown in Eq. (1)). To address this, fine-tuning with experimental bulk data aligns pre-trained features with collective behavior. This process bridges static molecular geometry with bulk phenomena, correcting single-molecule limitations and enabling accurate predictions despite collective-effect complexity.During the prediction process, it is found that the dielectric constant of a given carboxylic acid is lower than that of its isomeric esters even though the carboxilic group seems “more polar” compared to the ester group. As shown in Table S2, the predicted dielectric constants for butanoic acid, methyl propanoate, ethyl acetate, and propyl methanoate are 2.990, 6.017, 6.266, and 6.973, respectively, which are highly consistent with the corresponding experimental values measured at 303K. Similar observations can be found in other carboxylic acids and their corresponding isomeric esters as demonstrated in Table S1. This seemingly counterintuitive phenomenon can be ascribed to two aspects. First, the molecular dipole moment of the carboxylic acid is actually lower than that of its isomeric esters. As shown in Fig. 2d, although the carboxylic group itself possesses a more polarized charge distribution than the ester group does, the interaction between the positively charged protonic hydrogen and the negatively charged carbonyl oxygen within the carboxylic acid effectively counterbalances the overall molecular dipole moment. Second, due to the intermolecular hydrogen bond, the condensed phase carboxylic acid contains plentiful “symmetric” dimer structures (with a remarkably low dipole moment ~ 0.6 Debye based on density functional theory calculation) as shown in Fig. 2e, which lowers the overall polarity and hence the dielectric constant.Prediction of the mechanical and thermal propertiesWe now examine the capability of Org-Mol in predicting the viscosity, one of the crucial metrics in fluid mechanics. Note that compared with the dielectric constant, the viscosity is more sensitive to the temperature. Therefore, we carry out two separate fine-tuning jobs based on the pre-trained model with two sets of kinematic viscosities of various organic liquids measured at 40 °C and 100 °C, respectively. Note also that the relationship between the dynamic viscosity μ and the kinematic viscosity ν is μ = ν × ρ, where ρ is the density42. To enable the prediction for both the dynamic viscosity and the kinematic viscosity as well as the transformation between them, we also carry out a multi-regression fine-tuning task to predict the density of organic compounds at 25 °C, 40 °C, 60 °C, and 100 °C.It can be seen in Fig. 3a–d that the predicted values of the kinematic viscosity at two tested temperatures are highly consistent with the corresponding experimental counterparts. The R2 values for the train and test set of the kinematic viscosity at 40 °C are 0.991 and 0.972, respectively, while those at 100 °C are even higher (0.996 and 0.974, respectively). As shown in Fig. 3e, f and Fig. S2, the predicted densities are in extremely good agreement with the target values for both the train set and the test set. Compared to the prediction of dielectric constant and the viscosity, predicting the density is less difficult, due to the fact that the latter is a pure structural property and is less relevant to the dynamical behavior of the system. The slight underestimation of densities in high-density regions can be attributed to the sparsity of experimental data in those areas. In practice, very few common organic liquids reach such elevated densities, thus mitigating any significant impact on potential material design and selection processes.Fig. 3: Org-Mol model’s performance in predicting kinematic viscosity and density.Full size imagea, b The correlation between Org-Mol predicted kinematic viscosity at 40 °C and experimental counterparts for the training set and the test set, respectively. c, d The correlation between Org-Mol predicted kinematic viscosity at 100 °C and experimental counterparts for the training set and the test set, respectively. e, f The correlation between Org-Mol predicted density at 40 °C and experimental counterparts for the training set and the test set, respectively.For thermal properties, we first take the specific heat at constant pressure Cp (or the heat capacity), and the thermal conductivity κ as two representatives to examine the performance of Org-Mol. As shown in Fig. 4a–d, the correlation between the Org-Mol predicted values and the experimental counterparts for both of these two thermal properties remains high. The R2 values for the training and test sets are 0.993 and 0.982 for the heat capacity, respectively, with very small MAEs, evincing the capability of Org-Mol in the accurate prediction of thermal properties. Note that even though only 252 data points are collected for thermal conductivity, the performance of Org-Mol on the test set is still satisfactory (with the R2 values 0.958 for the test set), demonstrating its strength of tackling data with relatively small sample size. Furthermore, we assess the ability of Org-Mol in predicting properties of polymer systems by taking the glass transition temperature (Tg) as an example. We fine-tune Org-Mol on Tg data for around 300 homopolymers using repeating-unit structures as input (capping by hydrogen). As shown in Fig. 4e and f, the model achieves an R2 of 0.926 and MAE of 25.4K on the test set, outperforming previously reported MD-based predictions43 and demonstrating the potential generalizability of Org-Mol to homopolymer systems. It should be noted that predicting complex polymer properties remains challenging, especially for more sophisticated properties and those of copolymers, and specialized models like MMPolymer44 or PolyBERT45 are better suited for such scenarios.Fig. 4: Org-Mol model’s performance in predicting thermal properties.Full size imagea, b The correlation between Org-Mol predicted heat capacity and experimental counterparts for the training set and the test set, respectively. c, d The correlation between Org-Mol predicted thermal conductivity and experimental counterparts for the training set and the test set, respectively. e, f The correlation between Org-Mol predicted glass transition temperature of homopolymers and their experimental counterparts for the training set and the test set, respectively.Comparison with reference modelsTo validate the accuracy of Org-Mol across the aforementioned properties of organic small molecules, we conduct comparative experiments using three state-of-the-art methods: two graph neural networks (EGNN46 and NequIP47), and a tree-based algorithm (XGBoost48) with Morgan fingerprints as molecular descriptors. Hyperparameters are optimized for each model to ensure fair comparison. The metrics for the test set are summarized in Table 2. While graph neural network algorithms (EGNN and NequIP) outperform the tree-based model XGBoost, Org-Mol demonstrates superior performance across all evaluated properties. Notably, substantial enhancements are observed for dielectric constant and thermal conductivity, two properties inherently challenging due to their complexity and sparse experimental data, underscoring the efficacy of Org-Mol’s pre-trained architecture in handling complex and/or data-scarce scenarios.Table 2 Metrics of Org-Mol, EGNN, NequIP, and XGBoost for the dielectric constant ε, the kinematic viscosity ν at 40°C and 100°C, the heat capacity Cp, and the thermal conductivity κ.aFull size tableThe heat capacity of organic compounds, being a fairly predictable characteristic, has been thoroughly investigated using a multitude of ML techniques24,49. As summarized in Table 3, while previously reported models have gain relatively satisfying accuracies in predicting the heat capacity of various organics, Org-Mol achieves the highest accuracy among all applied algorithms (with marginal improvement compared to EGNN and NequIP as shown in Table 2) over a larger and more diverse dataset.Table 3 Comparison of previously reported models and this work for the heat capacity CpFull size tableTo further validate Org-Mol’s generalizability and prediction accuracy, we adopt a sphere-exclusion partitioning strategy (detailed in the Supporting Information) for all tested properties, representing a more rigorous test than random splitting. As shown in Fig. S4, the model maintained consistently high R2 values (>0.90) for small organic molecule property predictions, with the exception of dielectric constant (R2=0.876). In particular, this discrepancy arises from a single outlier. Excluding this point improves the R2 to 0.945, likely attributed to experimental measurement error. For homopolymer glass transition temperature prediction, the sphere-exclusion split test set yielded an R2 of 0.892, slightly lower than random partitioning results but still robust. Overall, Org-Mol achieves satisfying R2 scores across all properties under the more challenging sphere-exclusion scheme, underscoring its robust generalizability within the numerical bounds of the training data. We focus on synthetic esters for the design of novel immersion coolants owing to their extraordinary biodegradability. Due to its strict limit for immersion coolants, we apply the dielectric constant as a primary criterion and screen out over 6 million saturated monoesters and dibasic esters (constructed from saturated acid and alcohol, checked out from PubChem50) with the number of carbon atoms lower or equal to 30. Interestingly, all tested dibasic esters possess dielectric constants larger than 3.50, while 8569 monoesters meet the criterion. The corresponding t-SNE analysis is applied to the predicted dielectric constants of these monoesters to further justify the effectiveness of both the pre-trained and the fine-tuned model. As shown in Fig. 5a), with the randomly initialized weight, data points are evenly distributed with the 2D projected space. The distribution after pre-training, as seen in Fig. 5b), is capable of effectively distinguishing certain structures. Leveraging the power of 3D transformer-based algorithms, we have successfully fine-tuned the Org-Mol pre-trained model, achieving R2 values exceeding 0.95 for test sets across various physical properties of pure organic small molecules. Furthermore, Org-Mol’s ability to predict glass transition temperatures of homopolymers using repeating-unit structures (test set R2 > 0.92) highlights its potential for polymeric systems. This high level of accuracy not only surpasses current state-of-the-art models but also offers a practical solution to the challenges posed by traditional experimental methods, which are often costly and time-consuming.The application of Org-Mol in high-throughput screening has demonstrated its capability to enable the rapid identification of potential immersion coolants from a pool of millions of automatically constructed ester molecules. The experimental validation of two promising candidates further underscores the practical utility of our approach in accelerating the discovery of new materials for energy-efficient applications.To summarize, the Org-Mol model provides an important advancement in predicting properties of pure organic compounds, with far-reaching implications for energy-saving applications. Although the scope of the current work is limited to single-component systems, the demonstrated accuracy in predicting electrical, mechanical, and thermal properties-including its generalization to homopolymer glass transition temperatures—offers a foundational framework for rational design of tailored amorphous materials, as evinced by the experimental validation of immersion cooling candidates for energy-efficient electronics. While challenges in complex assemblies (e.g., mixtures, copolymers) necessitate further innovation, the model’s modularity and performance in pure organics paves the way for guiding the design of novel energy-efficient materials.MethodsModel constructionWe apply the framework of Uni-Mol to construct a pre-trained model, particularly designed for organic molecules containing C, H, O, N, S, Se, B, and halogens, namely the Org-Mol pre-trained model. Abstract
Accurate prediction of thermophysical properties is crucial for the rational design of lubricants and cooling fluids. We compile a database of approximately 4700 critically evaluated reference values for the density, viscosity, and thermal conductivity of 835 unique organic molecules in the C10–C50 range. We use this database to train and benchmark a range of machine learning (ML) architectures and molecular representations. XGBoost models trained on molecular descriptors are consistently among the most accurate across all three target properties. Out-of-distribution tests show that descriptor-space distance and the position of the predicted value within the training range identify higher-risk regions at the population level, rather than ordering the errors of individual molecules. Equilibrium molecular dynamics (EMD) simulations of eight representative molecules reproduce density accurately but show systematic, chemistry-dependent force-field errors for the viscosity and thermal conductivity. At an inference cost orders of magnitude lower than EMD simulations, the ML models are well suited to high-throughput screening of new candidate molecules for lubricants and other formulated products.
Machine learning models trained on ∼4700 reference values predict the density, viscosity, and thermal conductivity of lubricant-sized organic molecules, benchmarked against Green–Kubo molecular dynamics simulations of eight representative fluids.Introduction
Thermophysical properties such as the density, viscosity, and thermal conductivity of organic molecules are important to the performance of liquid formulations such as lubricants and refrigerants.1 Accurate prediction of these properties for pure organic molecules is also important for a wide range of industries, including energy, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals.2–4 In this context, the lack of reliable thermophysical data is one of the largest stumbling blocks in rational molecular,5 formulation,6 and process7 design. In particular, lubricants are required to adhere to strict viscosity limits across a wide temperature range (40–100 °C);8 however, for the organic molecules relevant to this application (C10–C50),9 viscosity–temperature data are still lacking. Viscosity data are available for many normal alkanes up to ∼C24, but data for branched alkanes, cycloalkanes, aromatics, alkyl cycloalkanes, and alkyl aromatics is much more sparse.10 There is also a lack of reliable thermophysical data available for oxygen-containing molecules such as esters, ethers, and glycols in the C10–C50 range.11 It is often possible to interpolate between missing entries with calculated predictions using a reliable equation of state, such as the perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT).12,13 Several other predictive models are available for pure hydrocarbons,14 with the most promising being group contribution and particularly entropy scaling methods.15,16 Quantitative structure–property relationship (QSPR) models17–21 have also been identified that are capable of predicting the viscosity of organic liquids. Within the chemical families and conditions for which they are parameterized, these methods can be highly accurate; their main limitation is reduced transferability, with predictive performance degrading outside the molecules and conditions for which experimental data are available.14 This makes extrapolation beyond the experimentally gathered dataset to new molecules or conditions less reliable. A quantitative comparison between these physically based methods and the machine learning models benchmarked here would require method-specific parameterization across the full dataset, and is left for future work.
Over the last few decades, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have become established as a useful tool with which to predict thermophysical properties and generate reliable datasets.22 MD simulations can in principle be applied to any organic liquid for which the molecular structure is known and a suitable force field is available, with an accuracy set by the force field and the sampling.23,24 The accuracy of force fields for MD simulations of the thermophysical properties of small molecules25 and linear and branched hydrocarbons has recently been studied.26 However, this type of comparison is still lacking for other industrially important classes of organic molecules, such as those containing cycloalkane, aromatic, ester, and ether groups. MD simulations are now routinely used to calculate the shear viscosity of single-component,26–29 binary mixtures,30–34 and multi-component35–37 hydrocarbon fluids with high accuracy over a wide range of conditions. In most cases, viscosity calculations through MD simulations have been restricted to small molecules, typically linear or branched alkanes. This is because larger hydrocarbons generally have higher viscosities,38 which are more challenging to accurately quantify through MD simulations due to their longer relaxation times.39 While MD simulations have also been used to predict the density and viscosity of oxygen-containing molecules40,41 and their mixtures,42 there are far fewer studies than for aliphatic hydrocarbons.
Machine learning (ML) has also emerged as a useful tool for predicting the thermophysical properties of pure organic liquids43 and their mixtures.44 Accurate viscosity prediction has been achieved using ML models such as artificial neural networks for single-component,45–51 binary mixtures,52 and multi-component53,54 organic liquids. ML methods have also been shown to be effective in predicting the viscosity of more complex molecules, such as ionic liquids55 and deep eutectic solvents.56 As with QSPR models, the performance of ML models remains at the mercy of accurate training data availability, with small, sparse or noisy datasets all having adverse effects on model accuracy. Even the largest available datasets on the thermophysical properties of fluids, such as the NIST REFPROP database,57 are sparse and subject to considerable uncertainties compared to other popular applications of ML.43
Some recent studies have combined MD and ML by using dynamic descriptors from the MD simulations to improve ML predictions of various fluid properties.58,59 In other cases, MD simulations have been used to generate reliable datasets with which to train ML models that can then be used for fluid property prediction.60,61 MD simulations have also been used to generate large databases of viscosity values, which have then been used to optimize the molecular structure of lubricants with high viscosity index using ML methods.5 A combination of MD simulations and ML has also been used to facilitate the data-driven design of polymer-based viscosity index improver additives.62 A recent study compiled a large experimental database containing viscosity values for 6120 small organic liquids59,63 and used this to train ML models to predict viscosity.64 They found that the ML prediction models outperformed MD simulations across a range of molecules and temperatures.64 A combination of ML and MD simulations was recently employed to predict the density, kinematic viscosity, thermal conductivity, specific heat capacity, and dielectric constant of esters in the context of immersion cooling fluids.65 Both MD simulations66 and ML models67 have been considered for thermophysical property prediction for decades; however, only relatively recent advances in computational hardware and software have made this type of wide parameter study feasible.22 However, systematic side-by-side evaluations of the two approaches on common sets of fuel- and lubricant-sized organic molecules remain scarce.
In this study, we benchmark ML models for the prediction of the density, viscosity, and thermal conductivity of lubricant-relevant organic liquids, and use MD simulations on a representative subset as an independent, physics-based assessment of the same properties. The primary aim is to develop ML models suitable for high-throughput virtual screening62,68 and molecular discovery5,69 workflows for high-performance lubricants. The MD simulations serve a complementary purpose, probing where and why physics-based prediction succeeds or fails for these types of molecules.
We evaluate 26 combinations of model architecture and molecular representation on approximately 4700 critically evaluated reference values for 835 fuel and lubricant-sized molecules, to identify the most accurate combination for each property. Because screening is most valuable beyond the chemistries that have already been measured, we then examine how far that accuracy extends to molecules unlike those seen in training, and which signals available at prediction time indicate where it does not. Finally, we apply Green–Kubo MD simulations to eight molecules, two from each of the four principal chemical families of the dataset, at 40 °C and 100 °C. This extends force field benchmarks that have concentrated on linear and branched alkanes26,28,29 to alkyl cycloalkanes, alkyl aromatics, esters, and ethers, for which experimental viscosity data remain sparse10 despite their importance in automotive fuels,70 aviation fuels,71 and lubricants.9,72Methodology
Machine learning models
To construct a robust and diverse dataset for model development and evaluation, we collected reference data for density, thermal conductivity and dynamic viscosity at atmospheric pressure and at both 40 °C and 100 °C. Only molecules with a dynamic viscosity of approximately 1–50 mPa s at 40 °C were included, because this is the range accessible to equilibrium molecular dynamics (EMD) simulations.39 Data were compiled from the Landolt–Börnstein series73 and the NIST Chemistry WebBook74 (accessed June 2024), resulting in 835 unique molecules carrying approximately 4700 critically evaluated reference values after the structure canonicalization, unit conversion and deduplication steps described below.
In cases where the properties of interest were not provided exactly at 40 °C or 100 °C, interpolation was used to obtain the values at these temperatures. The NIST WebBook74 utilizes a combination of property estimation methods to interpolate liquid viscosity values from the available experimental data. These include the PPDS9 (Physical Property Data Service) and ViscosityL correlations, which are based on semi-empirical and theoretical equations of state (extended Andrade models75,76) fitted from experimental values.4 The source method of every label is recorded, and the number of labels obtained by direct measurement versus by each database's own correlation or reference–property model is reported by property and temperature in Table S2. Most of the labels for density and thermal conductivity (99.0% and 97.8% at 40 °C) and approximately 44% of the viscosity labels are values produced by the source databases' own correlation, interpolation or reference–property models rather than direct measurements. The errors reported in this work therefore measure agreement with these adopted reference values, and do not include the uncertainty of the underlying database correlations. For molecules where both a direct measurement and a correlation value are available, the two agree closely across the full viscosity range at both temperatures (Fig. S1).
For interpolation of the liquid density values, the NIST WebBook uses the Tait equation.77 For liquid thermal conductivity, the TransportPolynomial model was applied, utilizing temperature-dependent polynomial fits to experimental thermal conductivity data. For the Landolt–Börnstein series,73 cubic spline interpolation using a minimum of three surrounding data points was employed to estimate the property values at the desired temperatures. In cases where only the kinematic viscosity was reported, it was converted to dynamic viscosity using µ = ν × ρ, where µ is dynamic viscosity, ν is kinematic viscosity, and ρ is density. Molecules whose viscosity was reported only as kinematic and for which no density was available at the same temperature were excluded (283 molecules at each temperature). Canonicalization and deduplication of the 1187 source entries give 1114 unique molecules, of which 835 retain at least one usable label and form the dataset used here. The viscosity values were normalized by taking their natural logarithm to improve regression performance during ML training.54

Oxygen-containing molecules were included alongside the pure hydrocarbons because oxygenated lubricant-like molecules, such as synthetic esters,78 are an important part of the target application space, and both classes are represented in the MD benchmark below. In this study, we compare the most commonly used molecular representations on our reference dataset to see which enables ML models to perform best on transport property prediction tasks. Fig. 1 shows the different molecular representations used to train ML models in this study.
Fig. 1. The molecular representations used to train the ML models, illustrated for butylbenzene 138%.

Open in a new tabMolecular descriptors are numerical features that encode chemical, physical, and structural properties of molecules and are widely used for ML-based property prediction.79,80 In this study, descriptors were generated using the RDKit and Mordred Python libraries,80 yielding 1019 descriptors per molecule after removal of invalid, missing, and categorical features. Descriptor scaling was applied selectively based on model requirements. Z-score normalization was used for magnitude-sensitive models (SVM and k-NN), while no scaling was applied for tree-based models (random forest and XGBoost) to preserve the natural feature distributions and chemically meaningful thresholds.
Dimensionality-reduced embeddings provide a compact alternative to high-dimensional molecular descriptors by reducing noise and redundancy while retaining the most informative features.81 In this study, embeddings generated using principal component analysis (PCA) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) were evaluated across a range of dimensionalities to assess their impact on model performance, as both the choice of method and retained dimensionality can influence predictive accuracy. PCA and UMAP embeddings were used as inputs to ML models to compare linear and nonlinear dimensionality reduction strategies for molecular property prediction. A detailed analysis of embedding method and dimensionality effects, including root-mean-square error (RMSE) trends across properties and model types, is provided in the SI. Embeddings were generated using the scikit-learn and UMAP-learn libraries from z-score normalized molecular descriptors.
Molecular fingerprints are typically represented as 2D binary strings, where each bit indicates the presence or absence of a specific structural feature or substructure within a molecule. A widely used and generally high-performing fingerprint type is the extended-connectivity fingerprint (ECFP), with the Morgan fingerprint being a common example.82 In this study, ECFPs are generated using the Morgan Fingerprint implementation in RDKit.79 While prior work has examined optimal ECFP parameters for molecular similarity assessment,83 no studies have specifically focused on optimizing ECFP generation for the property prediction of fuel- and lubricant-sized organic molecules using ML models. Accordingly, this study evaluates a range of ECFP generation parameters to identify those that yield the best regression performance. A systematic analysis of fingerprint parameters, including radius, bit size, and hashed versus unhashed representations,83 is provided in the SI.
Molecular graphs encode information about molecules by representing atoms as nodes and the bonds between them as edges. Nodes can be characterized by atom-level features such as atomic number, while the edges can incorporate bond-related characteristics such as bond type. Table S3 shows the features used to create molecular graphs in this study.
Simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) strings encode molecular structures as sequences of ASCII characters84 but are not inherently unique, as multiple valid strings can represent the same molecule. Canonical SMILES address this by enforcing a deterministic representation,85 although models trained on canonical SMILES may overfit to syntactic patterns rather than underlying chemistry.86 Despite this, SMILES remain widely used due to their simplicity and compatibility with sequence-based models such as CNNs and transformers.87 SELFIES (Self-Referencing Embedded Strings) were introduced to guarantee syntactic validity, ensuring that any token sequence corresponds to a chemically valid molecule.88 In this study, both canonical SMILES and SELFIES were evaluated as input representations for molecular property prediction. Strings were converted to token embeddings prior to model training; SMILES were generated from IUPAC names,89 and SELFIES were generated using the published SELFIES API.88
Pretrained transformer embeddings were obtained from ChemBERTa,90,91 a chemistry language model pretrained on large SMILES corpora. The frozen ChemBERTa-77M-MTR encoder was used as a fixed feature extractor. Each molecule's SMILES string is passed through the pretrained encoder and the token representations are mean-pooled (weighted by the attention mask) into a single fixed-length vector, with no fine-tuning of the encoder weights. These frozen embeddings were used as inputs to a multilayer perceptron (MLP) head and to an XGBoost model, providing a transfer-learning representation that complements the descriptor-, fingerprint-, and string-based inputs above.
In this study, we evaluate a range of models using the collated dataset to identify the most suitable algorithm for property prediction. The classic ML models, including support vector machines (SVMs),92 random forests (RFs),93 and k-nearest neighbors (k-NN),94 are implemented using the scikit-learn package in Python.95 XGBoost (Extreme Gradient Boosting) models were trained using the XGBoost Python library.96 The graph-based models, message passing neural networks (MPNNs)97 and graph attention networks (GATs),98 are implemented with the PyTorch Geometric library.99 The deep learning models, convolutional neural networks (CNNs),100 multilayer perceptrons,101 and transformers87 were implemented with the PyTorch library.99 ChemBERTa90,91 was evaluated in two configurations using the HuggingFace Transformers library: fine-tuning the full pretrained encoder end-to-end on SMILES, and the frozen-embedding configuration described above, in which only a small MLP head is trained on the fixed mean-pooled encoder output.
All models were evaluated under a single shared nested cross-validation protocol, applied to molecular representation configurations that were fixed in advance. The embedding dimensionality and the fingerprint radius and bit size were chosen by grid search on a single 80 : 10 : 10 train/validation/test split, as reported in the SI, so the protocol is nested with respect to hyperparameter selection and conditional on those representation configurations. The dataset was partitioned into five fixed outer folds, so that both temperatures of a given molecule always fall in the same fold and no molecule appears in more than one outer test set. The folds were constructed by stratified sampling over quintiles of the log-transformed 40 °C viscosity labels (molecules without a viscosity label were assigned via median-filled strata), then frozen. For each outer fold, hyperparameters were selected by random search over 25 configurations sampled from model-specific ranges, scored on a designated validation partition of the non-test data (approximately 85 : 15 train/validation); the selected configuration was then retrained on all non-test data and evaluated once on the untouched outer test fold. Full details of the architectures, hyperparameter ranges, and training procedures for each model are provided in the SI.Molecular dynamics simulations
The molecular structures of the eight molecules selected for this benchmarking study are shown in Fig. 2. These molecules were chosen to span the principal chemical families encountered in the reference dataset used in this work. All the MD simulations were performed using the LAMMPS software.102 EMD simulations were employed to calculate the density, viscosity, and thermal conductivity of the eight target molecules at 40 °C and 100 °C, consistent with conditions used to determine lubricant viscosity index values.8 All simulations were performed using the LOPLS-AA force field.103 Parameters for the LOPLS simulations were taken from Jorgensen et al.104 and Siu et al.103 Where required, the ester extension to LOPLS-AA was employed,105 while aromatic and ether parameters were taken from the corresponding OPLS-AA parameterizations. LOPLS-AA was selected because previous benchmarks have demonstrated it to be among the most accurate all-atom force fields for reproducing the experimental density and viscosity of linear hydrocarbons, including n-hexadecane,28n-dodecane, and n-octacosane.29

Open in a new tabInitial single molecule geometries were generated from the SMILES strings in RDKit by adding explicit hydrogens, embedding with the ETKDGv3 distance geometry algorithm,106 and minimizing with UFF. Cubic starting configurations were assembled with Packmol107 at a low initial density (0.3 g cm−3), with molecule counts selected to give approximately 15 000 atoms per box (163–349 molecules, depending on molecular size), corresponding to equilibrated cubic box lengths of 5.2–5.5 nm. A dedicated system size sensitivity study was not performed here, since all systems are well above the range where finite-size effects would be expected to affect the viscosity39 and thermal conductivity.108 Periodic boundary conditions were applied in all three Cartesian directions.
The protocol suggested by Schmitt et al.26 was adopted in the EMD simulations because it has been shown to enable accurate calculation of the viscosity of lubricant-sized molecules. A velocity–Verlet integrator with a 1.0 fs timestep was employed.109 Bonds containing hydrogen atoms were constrained with the SHAKE algorithm.110 Constraining C–H bonds is important for obtaining accurate thermal conductivities with all-atom force fields, as it suppresses the classically over-excited high-frequency C–H stretching modes that otherwise inflate the Green–Kubo heat flux.111 Lennard-Jones interactions were truncated at 12 Å with long-range tail corrections applied to energy and pressure, and long-range electrostatics were treated using the particle–particle particle–mesh (PPPM) method112 with a relative accuracy of 10−5. Geometric mixing rules were used for the unlike-atom interactions, and intramolecular 1–4 interactions were scaled by 0.5 following the OPLS convention.
The system was first relaxed by conjugate gradient energy minimization, followed by a short displacement-capped Langevin dynamics stage to remove any remaining close contacts. An equilibration in the canonical (NVT) ensemble was then performed at the target temperature to allow the system to reach thermal equilibrium. The density was then equilibrated at 1.0 atm and the target temperature for 1.0 ns in the isothermal–isobaric (NPT) ensemble using the Nosé–Hoover thermostat and barostat113,114 with damping coefficients of 100 fs and 1000 fs, respectively. The density was obtained directly as the ensemble averaged mass density at atmospheric pressure over the final 0.25 ns of the NPT trajectory, where a steady-state value had been reached.26 Density uncertainties were estimated as five-block standard deviations over this averaging window and are at most 0.003 g cm−3 (≤0.4%) for every state point. The simulation box was then deformed isotropically over 0.5 ns at constant temperature until the fluid density matched this average value. For each molecule, 10 independent replicas were branched from the equilibrated configuration with independently seeded velocities, each given a 0.2 ns NVT warm-up before production. Production was carried out in the NVT ensemble for 8 ns per replica to allow the slow shear-stress autocorrelation tail to converge.26
Viscosity was calculated using the Green–Kubo (GK) formalism,115,116 which is well suited to low and moderate viscosity fluids (<50 mPa s).39 The GK expression for the shear viscosity is:

where η is the viscosity, V is the system volume, kB is the Boltzmann constant, T is the temperature, and σαβ(t) is an off-diagonal component of the stress tensor at time t (with α and β denoting Cartesian directions x, y, or z); the angle brackets denote the stress autocorrelation function (ACF) averaged over time origins. To maximize the statistical sampling, the viscosity was averaged over all six independent components of the pressure tensor, combining the three off-diagonal terms with the three diagonal-difference terms, as recommended by Maginn et al.39
The time decomposition method (TDM) of Zhang et al.117 was used to improve the reliability of the calculations for the high-viscosity molecules. The time evolution of the running integral η(t) was recorded over the full production trajectory of each replica, with the stress ACF evaluated using a fast Fourier transform (FFT) technique.118 A cutoff time tcut was applied to the integral to mitigate accumulation of long-time noise, determined from the ratio of the standard deviation ση(t) across replicas to the average running viscosity:117matching the criterion of Schmitt et al.,26 who showed that ratios of ση/ηfinal between 0.2 and 0.8 do not materially affect the extracted values. The bootstrapping method,119 with 200 iterations, was used to compute the final viscosity value and its uncertainty, following the time-decomposition procedure of the PyLaT software120 and implemented in the released analysis script. Random combinations of the 10 replicas were resampled with replacement, and for each combination the replica-averaged running viscosity η̄(t) was fitted with the double-exponential function of eqn (2), in which η∞ is the long-time viscosity limit and α, β1, and β2 are fitting parameters:

This functional form reflects the physics of the underlying stress autocorrelation function, which decays through two distinct regimes: a fast relaxation associated with local, high-frequency stress fluctuations and a slow relaxation governed by collective, long-time structural rearrangement.117 The two exponential terms, with time constants β1 and β2 and relative weight α, capture these two modes, so that the running integral η(t) rises from zero and saturates toward the plateau value η∞, which is taken as the converged viscosity. Fitting to this form allows the well-sampled short-time behavior to determine η∞ while avoiding the accumulation of statistical noise in the poorly converged long-time tail of the integral, thereby providing a more robust estimate than reading off the running integral directly.39,117
The Green–Kubo formalism was also used to compute the thermal conductivity κ,121,122 from the autocorrelation of the microscopic heat flux vector Jq:


3

where κ is the thermal conductivity, Jq is the heat flux vector, the factor of three averages over the Cartesian components of the heat flux, and the angle brackets indicate a time-origin average of the autocorrelation function. The microscopic heat current was evaluated in LAMMPS using the centroid-based per-atom stress formulation of Surblys et al.123 for the pair, bond, angle, dihedral, and improper virial contributions. This formulation treats the many-body bonded interactions consistently in the heat-current expression, which is essential for obtaining accurate thermal conductivities in molecular systems with angle, dihedral, and improper terms.
As with the viscosity, the thermal conductivity was obtained from the running Green–Kubo integral κ(t), with the heat-flux ACF averaged over the three Cartesian components and evaluated by FFT.118 Unlike the shear stress, however, the heat-flux ACF carries no slow tail. The ACF decays to zero within a few picoseconds, so the running integral κ(t) reaches an early plateau and then drifts as statistical noise accumulates in the long-time tail. The double-exponential TDM fit used for the viscosity is therefore not required for the thermal conductivity, and integrating κ(t) to long lag times would only accumulate noise; the uncertainty of the Green–Kubo estimate grows with the upper integration limit relative to the total trajectory length,39 so the conductivity must be read from the short-time plateau rather than the converged integral. To locate this plateau without a hand-chosen cutoff, we first identified the lag time t* at which the normalized heat-flux ACF decays into its noise floor, defined as the first point beyond which its magnitude remains below twice the standard deviation of the long-time, noise-dominated tail. The thermal conductivity was then taken as the average of κ(t) over the window [t*, t* + 10 ps], immediately after the autocorrelation has decayed and before long-time noise sets in, with the reported value and uncertainty given by the mean and standard deviation of this window average across the 10 independent replicas.Results and discussion
Comparing ML models
Prior to benchmarking, we investigated embedding and fingerprinting strategies by systematic grid search on a single 80 : 10 : 10 train/validation/test split, with full details provided in the SI (Fig. S2–S5, Tables S4 and S5). For embeddings, PCA consistently outperformed UMAP across most properties and model types; one hypothesis is that its linear variance-preserving transformations suit the axis-aligned splits used by tree-based models, though the benchmark does not test this directly. Based on these results, PCA embeddings of 100 dimensions were used for all models. For fingerprints, increasing radius and bit size improved performance despite higher bit-collision rates, and unhashed Morgan fingerprints with a radius of 8 were selected as they eliminated collision-induced ambiguity and yielded the best overall predictive performance. Both comparisons rest on that single split and were not repeated within each outer fold, so they rank embedding and fingerprint configurations under one split rather than under the nested protocol.
All 26 model–representation combinations were then evaluated under the shared nested cross-validation protocol described in the Methods, using the same fixed outer folds for every model, representation and property. Conditional on the representation configurations fixed above, the quoted test errors are therefore free of test-set-tuned hyperparameter selection, although the outer folds serve as a comparative evaluation across the 26 combinations rather than a fully untouched holdout for the single winning model. All metrics reported below are means over the five outer folds, with the between-fold standard deviation as an estimate of their variability.
Table S6 reports the mean test RMSE and R2 for every model–representation combination, property and temperature; per-fold metrics, including mean absolute error (MAE) and the between-fold standard deviations, are provided with the released code. To identify the strongest models we z-score normalize the per-property RMSE values, invert them so that lower error corresponds to higher performance, and average across properties; we use this ranking only to select a common set of leading models and base all substantive claims on the property-specific results.

Open in a new tabXGBoost and RF models, when used with molecular descriptors, performed most consistently across all three transport properties. XGBoost with descriptors gave the lowest viscosity error of any combination (RMSE = 0.35 and 0.30 in ln(η/mPa s) at 40 and 100 °C, R2 = 0.86 and 0.83) and was among the best two or three combinations for density and thermal conductivity, while RF with descriptors gave the lowest density error (RMSE = 0.047 g cm−3). An error of 0.35 on the logarithmic scale corresponds to a typical discrepancy of a factor of 1.4 between predicted and measured viscosity. This aligns with previous studies,124,125 which also found tree-based models to be reliable across datasets. These methods handle nonlinear relationships and high-dimensional features effectively, making them suitable for the diverse information captured by molecular descriptors, and are relatively insensitive to feature scale, irregular target functions and uninformative features.126
When comparing representations for XGBoost, overall predictive performance followed the trend descriptors > PCA embeddings > ChemBERTa embeddings > fingerprints, and this ordering is particularly pronounced for viscosity, where the fingerprint model was substantially weaker (RMSE = 0.67 and 0.55; R2 = 0.51 and 0.42). This may be explained by the fact that while descriptors and PCA embeddings can incorporate both structural and physicochemical information, fingerprints are purely structural, lacking explicit encoding of global molecular properties, which limits their expressiveness for the transport properties considered here.
The SVM and k-NN models with molecular descriptors also achieved accuracy close to the leading tree-based models. SVM with descriptors reached a viscosity RMSE of 0.38 and 0.32 (R2 = 0.84 and 0.80), while k-NN with descriptors was clearly weaker at 0.44 and 0.36. For these distance-based models, descriptor and PCA embedding inputs gave comparable accuracy (for example, SVM viscosity RMSE of 0.38/0.32 with descriptors versus 0.38/0.31 with PCA embeddings). Some sensitivity to the high dimensionality and redundancy of descriptor sets is expected for distance-based methods,127 and may explain their larger errors relative to the tree-based models.
The GAT and MPNN models, trained on molecular graphs augmented with three-dimensional geometric information (bond lengths and partial charges derived from ETKDG conformers), were the weakest combinations, with GAT giving a viscosity RMSE of 0.78 and 0.63 (R2 = 0.33 and 0.22). This is notable given the theoretical advantages of geometric information for modeling molecular properties, and that graph ML methods have shown strong performance on related tasks.52,128 Two factors plausibly contribute: graph models typically require larger datasets than the one used here,129 and ETKDG conformers,106 while inexpensive, do not always capture the most energetically favorable geometry of flexible molecules, so the bond lengths and partial charges may only approximate the environments that govern transport properties. More accurate conformer generation, using density functional theory or machine-learning force fields, is therefore one route to improvement. Within this study the MPNN outperformed the GAT for every property and temperature, by 19 and 26% in viscosity RMSE at 40 and 100 °C and by 4 to 15% for density and thermal conductivity, on identical graphs and under the same search budget, although both remained well behind the descriptor-based models.
Among the deep-learning models, the transformer trained on the PCA molecular embeddings fell in the lower third of the benchmark (η RMSE 0.53 and 0.39; R2 = 0.69 and 0.70), well behind the MLP trained on the same embeddings (0.43 and 0.37), so the shortfall lies with the architecture rather than the representation. The two ChemBERTa91 configurations behaved very differently. Used as a frozen feature extractor, with only a small MLP head trained on the fixed mean-pooled embedding of each molecule, ChemBERTa was one of the strongest models overall. It gave the lowest thermal-conductivity error at 40 °C (RMSE = 0.0095 W m−1 K−1, R2 = 0.89) and consistent performance across all three properties, with viscosity accuracy (RMSE = 0.41 and 0.34) moderately behind the leading descriptor models. By contrast, fine-tuning the full ChemBERTa encoder end-to-end on SMILES predicted viscosity somewhat more accurately (RMSE = 0.37 and 0.31) but was markedly less consistent, with substantially larger density and thermal-conductivity errors (ρ R2 = 0.51). This pattern suggests that, on a dataset of this size, updating all encoder weights can overwrite useful pretrained features, whereas freezing them and learning only a lightweight head preserves the transferable representation and generalizes better.
A chemistry-pretrained transformer was thus among the best models for these transport properties when its pretrained embeddings were used directly. The comparatively poor SMILES fine-tuning is consistent with a distributional mismatch between ChemBERTa's predominantly drug-like pretraining corpus91,130 and the lubricant-sized molecules studied here, and points to parameter-efficient fine-tuning such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA),131 which freezes the base weights and introduces small trainable matrices, as a promising alternative, as demonstrated for other large chemistry and protein language models.132

        GROMACS 2024.1 on brand-new GPGPUs        
    
    
                     
                    
The first patch for the newest GROMACS version 2024 was released end of February. Recently, several new GPGPUs were added to the test cluster at NHR@FAU. As we benchmarked our usual set of six simulation systems, we decided to write a follow-up on our GROMACS benchmark posts (Multi-GPU GROMACS Jobs on TinyGPU and GROMACS performance on different GPU types) due to some interesting results on the latest hardware.



The Benchmarks




R-143a in hexane (20,248 atoms) with very high output rate,



a short RNA piece with explicit water (31,889 atoms),



a protein inside a membrane surrounded by explicit water (80,289 atoms),



a protein in explicit water (170,320 atoms),



a protein membrane channel with explicit water (615,924 atoms), and



a huge virus protein (1,066,628 atoms).




For running these benchmarks with GROMACS 2024.1 on a GPU, the following command was executed:



$ gmx mdrun -v -s $benchmark.tpr -nb gpu -pme gpu -bonded gpu -update gpu -ntmpi 1 -ntomp 16 -pin on \
   -pinstride 1 -nsteps 200000 -deffnm $benchmark_name



This offloads all possible calculations to the GPU and pins the program threads to CPU cores; the number of OpenMP threads depends on how many CPU cores are available. Since several GPUs are combined with one host CPU in Alex, each GPU has access to only a fraction of the host, which on Alex is 16 cores. The flags ‑nsteps, ‑v, and ‑deffnm are used for convenient benchmarking purposes and are not recommended in production runs; especially ‑v should only be used for debugging.



The (new) accelerators at NHR@FAU



NameArchitecture# CUDA coresPower consumptionRAMMemory bandwidthH100Hopper16,896700 W80 GB3.35 TB/sGH200Hopper16,8961,000 W96 GB4 TB/sA100Ampere  6,912400 W40 GB1.5 TB/sA40Ampere10,752300 W48 GB696 GB/sL40Ada Lovelace18,176300 W48 GB864 GB/sL40SAda Lovelace18,176350 W48 GB864 GB/s



Since GROMACS can only use the CUDA cores of the GPUs, the performance will correlate with that number; additionally, a higher power consumption usually means higher performance. The amount of RAM and memory bandwidth are no limiting factors for MD simulations of the listed benchmarks. Overall, the L40 and L40S should give the highest performance numbers due to the large number of CUDA cores.



The GPGPU benchmarks results



The results of the benchmarks with GROMACS 2024 on the new GPGPU hardware will be compared to the performance of the NVIDIA A40 and A100 GPGPUs that are both available in our Alex cluster. In particular, the A40 is ideal for MD simulation workloads due to its larger number of CUDA cores as compared to the A100.



[ns/day]System 1System 2System 3System 4System 5System 6A100267.5691.7265.8129.138.823.2A40277.0731.8268.1122.334.919.0



One of the reasons to switch to the latest GROMACS version are the continuous improvements in the code that by itself can already lead to slight performance increases. We had published a short article about that in the past. In fact, the performance increases from GROMACS 2023.2 on the A100 in Alex to the 2024 version are as follows:




System 1: 258.7 ns/day → 4%



System 2: 655.3 ns/day → 6 %



System 3: 260.3 ns/day → 1 %



System 4: 6ns/day → 2.0 %



System 5: 38.7 ns/day → 3 %



System 6: 23.2 ns/day → 0 %




Admittedly, the performance increases are not that big for the large systems but for the smaller ones it has an impact on overall simulation time. Moreover, switching from even older GROMACS versions can lead to larger performance improvements on the A100.



 GROMACS 2021GROMACS 2022.3System 1184.8 ns/day → 44.8 %241.7 ns/day → 10.7 %System 2613.2 ns/day → 12.8 %646.8 ns/day → 6.9 %System 3241.2 ns/day → 10.2 %248.8 ns/day → 6.8 %System 4122.8 ns/day → 5.1 %124.7 ns/day → 3.5 %System 537.6 ns/day → 3.2 %37.0 ns/day → 4.9 %System 621.9 ns/day → 5.9 %22.2 ns/day → 4.5 %



Similar performance improvements can be observed on the A40, too. Why stick to an older code version when the new code has improved algorithms for the exact same simulation method and, thus, optimizes time to solution?



As we have previously seen, small simulation systems yield higher performance on the A40 GPUs as compared to the A100, whereas larger systems benefit from the increased memory bandwidth of the A100. The explanation is simple: the number of atoms in the small systems is too small to properly saturate the GPU and thus, the communication between GPU and CPU is performance limiting. The observation that performance decreases with the amount of output is evident from the comparison of System 1 and System 2: albeit similar in system size, the former benchmark generates the energy output with a frequency 333x greater than the latter one and thereby loses performance by a factor of 2.6.



[ns/day]System 1System 2System 3System 4System 5System 6L40416.11254.7463.3212.157.831.7L40S405.31219.7472.4229.268.337.9



Both the A40 and A100 GPU have successors in the Ada Lovelace and Hopper architecture, respectively. For the A40, there are two versions of the Ada Lovelace generation: the L40 and the L40S; both have nearly identical specifications (18,176 CUDA cores, 48 GB RAM, and a memory bandwidth of 864 GB/s) and only the power consumption differs slightly: 300 W for the L40 and 350 W for the L40S. In theory, the more power is consumed, the faster the GPU clock, which leads to a larger overall performance. However, this is not true for the two small benchmarks. These two systems are not big enough to fully occupy the GPU, and communication slows down the performance. Moreover, the first benchmark has such a large output frequency that—even though its size is 2/3—the performance is roughly only a third of system 2. The same observation can also be made for all other GPUs, which is why we recommend setting up the NVIDIA MPS server for system with less than 50,000 atoms[1].



[ns/day]System 1System 2System 3System 4System 5System 6H100354.41032.8400.4205.063.537.5GH200411.51123.5470.6232.675.044.4



The successors of the A100 are the H100 and GH200, where the latter is an H100 in combination with an ARM-based NVIDIA Grace CPU. Both new GPUs have the same number of CUDA cores (16,896) but the specs for the GH200 are slightly increased compared to the H100: 700 W power consumption, 80 GB RAM, and a memory bandwidth of 3.35 TB/s, whereas the GH200 can consume up to 1,000 W, has 96 GB RAM, and a memory bandwidth of 4 TB/s. These differences as well as the close connection between CPU and GPU in the GH200 might be reflected in the performance numbers, as those for the GH200 are slightly better than those for the H100.



To compare the performance of GPUs in relation to the recommended GPU for MD simulations, namely the A40, we normalized the numbers by dividing the performance result for each GPU by that of the A40.

Now it becomes obvious that the small systems 1 and 2 and the smaller-sized medium system 3 should not be simulated on the A100 because the performance is lower than on the A40. In contrast, starting at approximately 150,000 atoms, it should be tested for each system if using the A100 is beneficial. Evidently, newer GPUs in combination with a recent GROMACS version increase performance significantly. However, it must be pointed out that the small systems can benefit more from the Ada Lovelace architecture than from the Hopper one and it should be vigorously tested if the performance gain is worth the extra procurement and maintenance cost of Hopper systems; more on that below.



For a more straightforward comparison of the GPUs that is independent from system size, we multiplied the performance by the number of atoms of the corresponding benchmark system. These numbers were then normalized to the A40 results and averaged.



\frac{\boldsymbol{[}\text{\textsf{\textbf{ns}}}\boldsymbol{/}\text{\textsf{\textbf{day}}}\boldsymbol{]}\boldsymbol{*}\text{\textsf{\textbf{atoms}}}}{\boldsymbol{[}\text{\textsf{\textbf{ns}}}\boldsymbol{/}\text{\textsf{\textbf{day}}}\boldsymbol{]\boldsymbol{*}\text{\textsf{\textbf{atoms}}}}_{\text{\textsf{\textbf{A40}}}}}AverageStandard DeviationH1001.610.26GH2001.860.34A1001.050.10A401.000.00L401.670.09L40S1.790.20



What we can see here is that in terms of performance gain, the Hopper and Ada Lovelace generations are so similar that a different metric is needed to decide which hardware should be used for MD simulations.



The additional metric we are going introduce is performance per hardware costs: the performance numbers have been divided by the hardware costs, standardized to the A40, and averaged. Some of the following GPU prices were taken from Deltacomputer in April 2024 and some in June 2024; VAT has been added manually.



\frac{\boldsymbol{[}\text{\textsf{\textbf{ns}}}\boldsymbol{/}\text{\textsf{\textbf{day}}}\boldsymbol{]}\boldsymbol{/}\text{\textsf{\textbf{costs}}}}{\boldsymbol{[}\text{\textsf{\textbf{ns}}}\boldsymbol{/}\text{\textsf{\textbf{day}}}\boldsymbol{]\boldsymbol{/}\text{\textsf{\textbf{costs}}}}_{\text{\textsf{\textbf{A40}}}}}CostsAverageH100€30,723.420.27GH200€29,750.000.32A100 €8,644.160.62A40 €5,087.251.00L40 €7,168.561.18L40S €7,259.001.25



Evidently, the prices for GPUs from the Hopper generation are several times higher than for the Ada Lovelace GPUs, but the performance gain does not reflect that. This analysis also reveals that the A40, as it is available in our Alex cluster, shows good performance in combination with a comparatively low price tag.



In summary, we have shown that while the Hopper generation looks promising for MD simulations in terms of CUDA cores and performance results, it does not yield higher performance than the GPUs from the Ada Lovelace architecture. Taking procurement costs into account, the L40 and L40S from the Ada Lovelace generation are much more attractive platforms for GROMACS users.
